intro: A sixteen-bar theme supports six variations, then returns without its accumulated decoration. The central problem is how far Beethoven can change rhythm, texture and register while keeping the theme’s harmonic outline audible.
question: What survives when a theme becomes almost unrecognisable?

cues.title: A theme with repeats
cues.text: The opening theme has sixteen bars in two repeated halves. Beethoven marks it “Gesangvoll, mit innigster Empfindung” — songfully, with the most inward feeling. Keep its phrase endings in mind: six variations will change the surface around that framework.
cues.evidence: The score gives the theme and its repeats. Quiet points around 0:35, 1:15, 1:50 and 2:30 help estimate its performed extent; the bars have not been aligned to this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Weight on beat two
cues.text: Through the theme, listen for the dotted rhythm’s emphasis on the second beat. This gives the three-beat phrases something of a sarabande’s shape, rather than the continuous lift of a waltz.
cues.evidence: This is a score-based listening suggestion for the whole theme, not an event located at 0:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Remember the harmonic route
cues.text: During the repeated theme, try to retain the bass movement and the places where the phrases settle. Those features provide points of comparison when the variations add decoration and quicker notes.
cues.evidence: The score repeats both halves of the theme. The recording’s quiet close around 2:30 provides an approximate outer limit for this opening span.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A higher singing line
cues.text: In the first variation, the melody moves into a higher register and acquires decoration. Compare its singing upper line with the more chordal opening theme; the harmonic resting points remain useful landmarks.
cues.evidence: The first variation follows the repeated theme in the score. A quiet gap around 2:30 and renewed activity from 2:35 suggest the transition, rather than establish a precise entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: For Maximiliane Brentano
cues.text: The sonata is dedicated to Maximiliane Brentano, daughter of Beethoven’s friends Franz and Antonie Brentano. He had already written a short piano trio for her in 1812.
cues.evidence: The dedication and earlier Trio, WoO 39, are documented in the work history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven)

cues.title: One variation, several textures
cues.text: The second variation combines short exchanges, imitation and more continuous accompaniment. Listen across the section for changes in how the hands divide the work: a variation need not maintain one pattern throughout.
cues.evidence: The score’s second variation contains these contrasting textures. A fall in recorded level around 4:05 supports an approximate start here; individual changes are not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Full phrases and gaps
cues.text: In this stretch, fuller phrases alternate with quieter, more separated writing. Listen for the contrast between the piano’s attacks and the resonance left between them.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a substantial fall in relative level from 4:35 to 4:55, followed by more detected attacks around 5:05–5:15. These measurements describe a span, not individual notes.

cues.title: A difficult first edition
cues.text: Schlesinger published the sonata in Berlin in 1821. The first edition contained numerous errors: Beethoven had supplied his difficult autograph rather than a clean copy, and illness interfered with his correction of the proofs.
cues.evidence: The work history documents the 1821 edition and its proofreading difficulties: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven)

cues.title: Two hands, independent lines
cues.text: Across the middle variations, listen to the lower part as a melody rather than simply an accompaniment. Beethoven uses counterpoint: distinct lines move together without always sharing the same rhythm.
cues.evidence: The middle variations contain two-part and more densely imitative writing. The analysis changes around 6:10–6:22, but does not securely identify every variation boundary.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Activity gives way
cues.text: This part of the movement alternates more active phrases with shorter withdrawals. Compare the speed of the small notes with the slower progress of the harmony underneath.
cues.evidence: Both relative level and detected attacks fall around 7:10, then rebuild through 7:30. The cue describes that surrounding contrast.

cues.title: Space between the phrases
cues.text: Listen through the quieter gaps as well as the fuller phrases. The resonance of an earlier chord can remain part of the music while the hands prepare their next attack.
cues.evidence: The report shows a quiet, sparsely attacked span around 8:20–8:25 and a substantial rise by 8:35; it does not identify the pianist’s pedalling.

cues.title: The pressure returns
cues.text: In this stretch, denser keyboard writing follows another withdrawal. The contrast prepares a larger change: the final variation will recover the theme’s slow pace before building activity again.
cues.evidence: Activity increases around 9:40–10:15, then recedes near 10:25. The score places the slow opening of the final variation after the contrapuntal variations.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final variation
cues.text: The final variation begins quietly at the theme’s tempo. Across this section, Beethoven divides the beat into progressively smaller notes until repeated movement becomes prolonged trilling.
cues.evidence: A fall in level and attacks around 10:25–10:30 suggests the final variation’s start. Its subdivision and trills are written in the score; their individual onsets are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Subdivision, not simply speed
cues.text: Follow the larger beat beneath the increasingly small notes. Beethoven can make the surface more active by fitting more notes into a beat, without requiring the harmonic rhythm to accelerate in the same proportion.
cues.evidence: The final variation’s written note values become progressively smaller. The report shows growing activity and level around 10:50–11:20, but is not a reliable beat tracker.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A trill becomes continuity
cues.text: Through the final variation’s trilled writing, rapidly repeated notes approach a sustained layer while other lines keep moving. Listen for the longer melodic shapes rather than trying to count each small attack.
cues.evidence: Prolonged trills belong to the score’s final variation. The sustained higher-level span around 11:15–12:05 is compatible with that placement, not proof of each trill’s timing.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The theme without decoration
cues.text: Near the end, the opening theme returns without the accumulated passagework. Compare its slow chords with the trills that preceded them: recognition, rather than another increase in activity, closes the sonata.
cues.evidence: After the retreat around 12:20–12:25, the recording resumes a sparse pattern resembling the opening. The score places the plain theme here; the return is estimated around 12:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No added peroration
cues.text: The closing cadence stays quiet, without another virtuoso flourish. Listen beyond the attacks to the remaining piano resonance.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls across 13:35–13:55, reaching silence around 14:00. This is a closing passage, not a precisely located final keystroke.

transitions.title: The fast counterpoint releases the theme
transitions.how: After the fifth variation’s fast imitative writing, Beethoven restores the theme’s tempo and changes from cut time to 3/4. E major remains the tonal frame: the join does not need a new key to make a new beginning. The hands relinquish their competing quick lines for the theme’s slower melodic and harmonic outline. This reduction is structural, not an ending: the sixth variation will rebuild the surface by dividing each beat into progressively smaller notes.
transitions.evidence: The listening map places the final variation at 626 s. The analysis marks a boundary at 10:26 and a fall in relative level and attacks at 10:25–10:30. The score changes from Variation V’s Allegro ma non troppo in cut time to Variation VI’s Tempo primo del tema in 3/4; the individual bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: The trill yields to plain chords
transitions.how: The final variation withdraws its prolonged trills and quick decoration rather than adding another virtuoso cadence. The original E-major theme then returns in its plain chordal texture, with the slow bass movement and dotted melodic rhythm exposed again. No contrasting key or new theme separates the two states: Beethoven removes the accumulated activity until the opening becomes recognisable. The restored theme is given without its original repeats, so recollection now leads directly towards the quiet close.
transitions.evidence: The section boundary is 750 s. Relative level retreats through 12:20–12:25 before sparse attacks resume at 12:30; the form relation matches the opening at 752–768 s. The score restores the undecorated theme after Variation VI, without the opening repeats. These anchors establish a passage, not the exact release of a trill.

facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
